content.comment_body: Apologies if my explanation isn't perfect—I'm still learning as I go. I'm currently using a [product_name] for basic lighting automation at home. Could anyone advise on best practices for wiring the digital inputs? My idea was to run a lightweight wire from each room's switch box back to the [product_name]. For example, an eight-core 0.2mm communication cable, which could handle multiple switches per box and would be easy to install. The technical specifications for the [product_name] indicate only 0.08 mA is drawn for an 'on' signal, so I assumed this means there’s no need to worry about high current through the wires. I'm also not sure if voltage drop could be an issue because of the higher resistance in thinner wires. I don't entirely grasp this aspect and wonder whether thin wires themselves consume power like the filament in a bulb. Additionally, I’m assuming the [product_name] has high impedance on its inputs, otherwise it would draw more power when the input circuit is closed.
It's not safe to use communication cable for transmitting 230V AC signals. These cables do not meet the required specifications for 230V in terms of cross-sectional area and insulation.

analysis.insight_summary: A user is requesting advice on best practices for wiring digital inputs for home lighting automation using a [product_name], highlighting limited experience with electrical standards. There is uncertainty about current usage, voltage drop, and which wire type is suitable. Safety and compatibility between the [product_name] and thin multi-core communication wire are a primary concern. Another participant notes that standard communication cables are not suitable for 230V AC signals due to specification and insulation issues, pointing out a gap in safety knowledge.
analysis.user_expectations: The user wishes to receive straightforward and safe instructions for connecting digital inputs to a [product_name] using thin, multi-core cables, aiming for simplicity without compromising performance or safety. They expect confirmation that low current usage makes lightweight wiring acceptable and are seeking both assurance and a clearer understanding of the topic.
